text:
ANTALYA, Turkey — There’s an old adage in politics: never let a crisis go to waste. Yet governments at crucial U.N. climate talks just did exactly that.
The Antalya summit lurched to a chaotic conclusion Sunday when a draft deal on tackling global warming collapsed, despite a desperate scramble for an agreement which had already taken negotiations 48 hours over the scheduled finish.
Countries failed to strike a final agreement despite fresh scientific warnings and an energy price shock which many governments said offered more momentum than ever for ditching planet-heating fossil fuels.
That means countries are leaving Antalya after two weeks of intense negotiations with only a handful of technical agreements to their name. There is no political deal to show how they intend to pull the planet back from the verge of dangerous climate change.
U.N. climate chief Simon Stiell stressed that the summit made “real progress,” despite the lack of agreement on the main text (called the "cover decision").
“This ridiculous system of having absolute consensus, where 192 countries and 100,000 people who are here in Antalya agree on absolutely everything, it's a recipe for disaster,” Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama’s climate minister, told POLITICO earlier in the week. “COPs have turned into a laughing stock.”
Governments arrived in Turkey knowing the world stands on a precipice. This summit marked the first climate conference since the U.N. announced the world was sure to overshoot the target to limit long-term global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.
“The situation coming into this talk was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory, and also, in ways I very much sympathize with, the impacts of climate change [are] getting worse,” Australian Climate Minister Chris Bowen, who co-hosted the talks, told reporters Sunday.
Missing the 1.5C target, the Paris Agreement’s most ambitious aim, loomed large in Turkey. Many nations cited the impending overshoot as justification for agreements to make deeper cuts to pollution, take stronger action to prepare for disasters and increase financial support for poorer countries.
But countries rich in oil and gas resources fought to keep any mention of fossil fuels — the main cause of global warming — out of the final text, while wealthy nations were reluctant to commit to specific funding goals.
The final impasse that brought down the talks revolved around the future of energy. A coalition of 130 countries, led by the European Union and small island states, demanded the COP31 text include a reference to a three-year-old commitment to phase out fossil fuels. But that was too much for some petrostates. Even recommitting to this earlier agreement was a red line for countries such as Saudi Arabia.
Another point of conflict was a paragraph in earlier drafts of the deal that appeared to put contentious carbon capture technologies on equal footing with clean power sources such as renewables. The anti-fossils coalition wanted those references deleted, arguing they catered to Riyadh’s interests to prolong the use of oil and gas.
On Sunday, Saudi Arabia pushed back. “We cannot reconcile a position that stated so publicly that we need to keep 1.5 degrees within reach, and yet called carbon capture, utilization, and storage technologies greenwashing,” said country negotiator Mohammad Ayoub.
In a fractious final plenary session, the EU and small islands, alongside the United Kingdom, Norway, Switzerland, several Latin American nations and a group of the world’s poorest countries, rejected the deal drawn up by Turkey and Australia, the conference co-hosts.
“We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science, that disregards the implementation gap, and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required to correct the overshoot and bring 1.5 degrees back to within reach,” said Irish Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU.
“We will not endorse a cover decision,” he added, “that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time.”
All Turkish minister Murat Kurum, presiding over the talks, could do was admit defeat. He walked off the plenary floor not long after, before the conference — which had by then turned into the longest climate summit in its 30-year history — had ended.
Some pointed to deals made on the margins of the talks, in the so-called action agenda, as well as the conclusion of technical agreements, as evidence the U.N. climate process was still working.
“I share the disappointment of many,” Stiell told reporters Sunday evening. “We must also recognize that this COP process has two tracks, and across the action agenda COP31 has delivered real progress and concrete results.”
The conference was not always destined to end in disarray. The geopolitical momentum was on the Turkish-Australian presidency’s side.
Beside U.N. warnings about overshooting the 1.5°C barrier, the talks coincided with growing public anger over high fossil fuel prices caused by the Iran war. Many governments around the world, alarmed at rising costs of oil and gas imports over which they had little control, were already speeding up their switch to clean energy , citing affordability and sovereignty as well as climate action.
Co-hosts Australia and Turkey sought to harness that crisis through proposals to accelerate efforts to replace fuel-burning gasoline-powered cars with electric alternatives such as EVs.
But their proposed flagship target to increase electricity’s share in the world’s energy consumption from 23% today to 35% in 2035, included in the final draft text, was rejected along with everything else.
It was discussions around the electricity target that started the debate that, ultimately, led to the conference’s breakdown.
The International Energy Agency says that to reach net-zero emissions by the middle of this century — a key effort to meet the Paris Agreement goals — the global electrification rate must increase in line with that proposed target, but also that clean power like wind and solar must supply 90% of electricity by then — up from 42% today.
That pushed several countries to lobby for an agreement on “clean” electrification — to ensure that the electrification push does not open the door to more high-polluting coal, oil or gas.
“EU citizens will not accept a fossil fuel COP,” a senior European official said Friday afternoon, warning of a “no-deal scenario” over “insufficient language on clean electrification” in a draft version of the accord.
The EU then teamed up with small island states and dozens of other nations that had backed a push for exiting fossil fuels at last year’s conference in Brazil. Together, the gang of more than 100 nations marched into the presidency offices on Saturday night to state their demands: a reference to the previous energy transition agreement and the deletion of the Saudi-linked carbon capture text.
When tweaks to the text during the final plenary did not deliver what they wanted, many of these countries rejected the text outright.
“We came here expecting the world to deliver a comprehensive and urgent response on reducing emissions, on protecting our people, and on providing the finance to do this,” said Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, a negotiator for the Marshall Islands. “We have been let down on all sides.”
Not all countries rejected the text. China, India and a group of African nations said they would not stand in the way of its adoption. U.N. climate summit decisions, however, require consensus from all the nearly 200 nations in attendance.
Discontent with the Australian-Turkish co-hosts started brewing early this week.
A first draft of the deal — a laundry list of all possible demands from countries — baffled many national delegations when it was published on Monday. A second draft only came on Thursday, setting off days of shuttle diplomacy behind closed doors.
After many delays, a third and supposedly final draft decision appeared just after midnight Sunday, long after the conference was meant to wrap. Exhausted and disgruntled diplomats were by then in no mood to make further concessions.
“The process is basically mismanaged,” Xolisa Joseph Ngwadla, an adviser to the chair of the African negotiating group, told reporters Saturday. “We haven’t seen text in more than 48 hours. We haven’t met as all parties in more than three days. We’ve all seen just snippets of text. That’s not conducive to a transparent and inclusive process to work towards an outcome. You don’t get an outcome like that.”
But the conference backdrop also spelled trouble. The stakes were low — while Australia and Turkey insisted on pushing for a political agreement, no blockbuster deal needed to be done.
It was all happening while geopolitical tensions soared amid wars in Iran and Ukraine. A rising far right and tight budgets at home put many rich countries on the defensive — while many developing countries, reeling from worsening climate disasters and mounting debt, demanded more financial support.
The EU, smarting from last year’s conference where it was left isolated pushing for more climate action, was gearing up for a fight.
And the absence of the United States from the process, after President Donald Trump withdrew his country for the second time, shifted the power dynamics toward emerging economies. Privately, several European diplomats said that with the “old U.S.” in the room, Saudi Arabia could have been contained.
The draft deal would also have done little to address the overshoot of 1.5°C, which scientists say can be brought back under control only through dramatic emissions cuts and large-scale deployment of technologies for sucking carbon from the atmosphere. Most such tech is unproven to work at the scale required.
European diplomats said Saudi Arabia even questioned the science behind the overshoot, suggesting that research is not settled unless it appeared in reports of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change — while simultaneously allegedly trying to delay future reports from the IPCC. The Saudi energy ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
An attempt to resolve the standoff over science, injected into the presidency’s draft decision, failed alongside the rest of the text.
The talks also collided with skyrocketing global electricity demand, driven by the sudden expansion of data centers, modernizing economies and an explosive uptake in electric cars worldwide .
Artificial intelligence alone poses new risks to international climate efforts, as tech companies increasingly use natural gas to run new power plants dedicated to data centers’ massive compute capacity. Yet the summit barely addressed those growing climate threats .
Some negotiators tried to put a quick brave face on the collapse.
The EU and Britain both insisted they would continue pushing for global climate agreements. “Our position is not a rejection of multilateralism, but a defence of multilateralism that delivers,” Ireland’s O’Brien and the bloc’s climate chief Wopke Hoekstra said in a joint statement.
“History will not judge COP31 by whether a decision was adopted, but by whether the international community rose to the challenge of our time,” they added.
